bib.title: HtmlRAG: HTML is Better Than Plain Text for Modeling Retrieved Knowledge in RAG Systems
bib.venue: WWW '25 (Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2025)

question: Does keeping retrieved web pages as (cleaned, pruned) HTML instead of plain text improve RAG answer quality?
hypothesis: HTML preserves structural and semantic information lost in plain-text conversion, and LLMs can already read it without fine-tuning.
contributions: Propose HTML as the format of knowledge in RAG systems
A simple but effective HTML cleaning algorithm
A two-stage (embedding then generative) block-tree HTML pruning algorithm

method.summary: Retrieved web pages are cleaned by rules (drop CSS/JS/comments, long attributes, merge single-nested tags, drop empty tags), parsed to a block tree (max words per block), pruned greedily by BGE similarity at 256-word blocks, then by a fine-tuned Phi-3.5-mini path-generation model at 128-word blocks that scores blocks by token-tree generation probability. The pruned HTML (4K tokens) is fed to Llama-3.1 readers.
method.task: Open-domain QA over Bing-retrieved web HTML (post-retrieval refinement)

limits: Weaker pruner scaling study (Appendix D) is 'very preliminary'; only two pruners tried.
The 70B gain over BGE is small or null on several metrics (Table 1); ELI5 ROUGE/BLEU show no advantage (HtmlRAG 15.51/5.84 vs BGE 15.87/6.30 at 8B).
At 128K, HTML without pruning ties plain text rather than beating it; HTML costs extra tokens under 4K windows.
Retrieval was Bing only, 400 questions per dataset, one run; no decoding settings or reader prompt reported.
Authors note the 70B reader is sometimes worse than 8B, attributing it to distraction by noise (Appendix E).
Training-data source datasets are not named.
